title: 2 Chronicles 27:1–9
context: Jotham reigns sixteen years and does what is right, like his father Uzziah, but he does not enter the LORD’s temple, while the people still act corruptly. He builds, fortifies, defeats the Ammonites, and grows strong because he ordered his ways before the LORD. The parallel in 2 Kings 15:32-38 is briefer: it mentions the upper gate and the high places that remained, and adds that in Jotham’s days the LORD began to send Rezin and Pekah against Judah. The note that he did not enter the temple, his other building, and the Ammonite tribute appear only in Chronicles. The dating of Jotham’s reign relative to other synchronisms in Kings is difficult, and interpreters reconstruct it in different ways.

verses.text: Jotham was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jerushah the daughter of Zadok.
verses.arminianNotes: Jotham begins to reign at twenty-five and reigns sixteen years. Arminian readers see a long reign as a wide door of opportunity, and they note his mother’s name, Jerushah, spelled Jerusha in 2 Kings 15:33.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the opening formula matches 2 Kings 15:33 apart from the spelling of his mother’s name. They see the standard pattern as framing a reign the Chronicler will evaluate by Jotham’s walk with God.

verses.text: He did that which was right in the LORD’s eyes, according to all that his father Uzziah had done. However he didn’t enter into the LORD’s temple. The people still acted corruptly.
verses.arminianNotes: Jotham does right like Uzziah, but he did not enter the LORD’s temple. Arminian readers see a king who learned from his father’s presumption (2 Chronicles 26:16), choosing restraint where Uzziah had overreached.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the note about the temple is not in 2 Kings 15:34, and they note the sad line, the people still acted corruptly. A faithful king could not by himself change the heart of the nation.

verses.text: He built the upper gate of the LORD’s house, and he built much on the wall of Ophel.
verses.arminianNotes: He built the upper gate of the LORD’s house and much on the wall of Ophel. Arminian readers see building as one way a faithful king expresses care for worship and for the safety of his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Kings 15:35 also mentions the upper gate, while the work on Ophel appears only here. Building projects in Chronicles often accompany a king’s faithfulness as signs of blessing.

verses.text: Moreover he built cities in the hill country of Judah, and in the forests he built fortresses and towers.
verses.arminianNotes: Jotham built cities in the hill country and fortresses and towers in the forests. Arminian readers see diligent stewardship, a king using the peace he was given to strengthen the land for the future.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this building program is described only in Chronicles. They read it as part of the blessing the Chronicler attributes to Jotham’s faithfulness, summed up in verse 6.

verses.text: He also fought with the king of the children of Ammon, and prevailed against them. The children of Ammon gave him the same year one hundred talents of silver, ten thousand cors of wheat, and ten thousand cors of barley. The children of Ammon also gave that much to him in the second year, and in the third.
verses.arminianNotes: He defeated the Ammonites, who paid tribute for three years. Arminian readers see success in war as one of the fruits of a reign ordered before God, while also noting that it is described soberly and briefly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the Ammonite war and the large tribute are not mentioned in Kings. The amounts reflect the Chronicler’s picture of a strong reign; the figures are recorded only here.

verses.text: So Jotham became mighty, because he ordered his ways before the LORD his God.
verses.arminianNotes: Jotham became mighty because he ordered his ways before the LORD. Arminian readers see a real link between faithful choices and blessing, while recognizing that the link is not a mechanical guarantee. The Leviticus 26:3 box discusses such conditions.
verses.reformedNotes: The 2 Kings 15:34 notes cite this verse as the reason for Jotham’s strength, and Reformed readers agree. They see the blessing as God’s gift to a king whose ways were set before him, and the Chronicler’s theme of faithfulness and prosperity on display.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Jotham, and all his wars and his ways, behold, they are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of Jotham’s acts, wars, and ways are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah. Arminian readers note that the record includes his ways, his moral character, not only his military deeds.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the Chronicler’s reference to a fuller source, which differs in title from the chronicles of the kings of Judah cited in 2 Kings 15:36. Its relation to Kings is discussed by interpreters.

verses.text: He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: “He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem.” These are the same facts given at the opening of the chapter. Arminian readers take the notice as a simple close to a short, approving account of the reign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as a regnal summary, not as a doctrinal point. Both traditions let the notice stand and turn to the succession that follows.

verses.text: Jotham slept with his fathers, and they buried him in David’s city; and Ahaz his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Jotham dies, is buried in David’s city, and Ahaz succeeds him. Arminian readers note, as the 2 Kings 15:38 notes do, that a faithful father does not guarantee a faithful son.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Chronicles omits the notice of 2 Kings 15:37 that the LORD began to send Rezin and Pekah against Judah in Jotham’s days. The threat will come into full view under Ahaz.
